Auctioning hands them the only monopoly that can be completed right now; they will outbid everyone. $350 blocks that. message.reasoning:
Evaluating the Monopoly property purchase decision.

I cannot afford both Park Place and Oriental Avenue. Buying the dark blue property would leave only $235, which is insufficient to purchase the missing light blue deed and build houses.

Auctioning the property is risky. Player 4 owns Boardwalk, so they could buy it to complete a dark blue monopoly. Even with cash left over, I cannot afford to develop the property.

Player 4 has $836 in cash. They would likely bid aggressively for Park Place at auction to complete the dark blue monopoly. That set is the most expensive in the game. Hotel rent on Boardwalk and Park Place reaches over $1,500 each. Blocking this acquisition is critical.

I can still buy Oriental Avenue for $100 and build two light blue houses with the remaining $135. The unimproved rent on Park Place is only $35, but blocking Player 4 from completing the dark blue monopoly is the dominant factor.

The $585 cash could buy Oriental and build three houses on each light blue property. That leaves $35. Buying Park Place would leave only two houses on the light blues. Standard light blue rent is $6, $30, $90, $270, $400, and $550.

Three houses on the light blues is the sweet spot. Two houses is weaker but still viable.

Player 4 could afford to pay $400 for Park Place at auction and still build two houses. That would not be immediately devastating.

Still, a dark blue monopoly wins almost every game over time.

Player 2 is missing the Kentucky and Atlantic railroads. Player 1 owns all four railroads plus St. Charles, but only St. Charles is part of the pink group; St. James and Tennessee are orange. Player 4 owns States and New York.

Player 2 owns Ventnor, Marvin Gardens, and Pacific. That is a full yellow monopoly. Player 2 also owns Indiana and Illinois, giving them two-thirds of the red group.

No player currently holds a full monopoly. Player 2 is closest on red and yellow, each missing only a bank deed. Player 4 owns Boardwalk, so acquiring Park Place at auction would instantly complete the dark blue set without waiting for a bank property.

Player 4 could pay $500 to $700 for Park Place at auction and still build. Buying the property now would block that immediate acquisition. I would retain two-thirds of the light blue group and could purchase Oriental later. I might trade Park Place for New York Avenue.

Auctioning is futile because Player 4 would win anyway. I can afford the $350 purchase and survive a single $200 railroad rent hit, but two hits would bankrupt me. Player 2's unimproved properties yield low rent, and no monopolies exist yet so base rent applies. Keeping Park Place permanently blocks Player 4 from completing the dark blue set.

Mortgaging Water Works, Vermont, or Connecticut could raise the $35 needed after a $200 railroad rent hit. The cash risk is manageable. I am also checking whether Player 4 might not bid aggressively for the property.

Player 4 will likely bid $400 to $600 for Park Place at auction. Buying it now at $350 is a clear value win, and blocking the acquisition is still worthwhile. Auctioning to drain Player 4's cash is possible but unlikely to stop them from winning the property.

The win path is to block the dark blue set, then buy Oriental and build light blues. Three houses on the light blues would yield $270 to $300 in rent, while two houses still provides solid income. With only $235 remaining after the purchase, I will need to wait for a future landing on Oriental to spend $100. Until then, I can collect rent from my existing properties and pass GO for $200. At turn 66, I am near the end of the board, so I may not land Oriental immediately.

From Park Place, a roll of 2 lands on Luxury Tax. A roll of 3 lands on Boardwalk for $50 rent to Player 4. Any higher roll passes GO for $200 and lands on other spaces. The next turn should recover cash quickly.
